name: Temple of Literature, Hanoi
label: Temple of Literature
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Văn Miếu Môn' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Văn Miếu Môn' (way/702185143): middle (14 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21422528: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Temple of Literature' (375 m across).
notes: Confucian temple and Vietnam's first university, founded in 1070.

text.description:
The Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu) is a Confucian temple that was first built in 1070. From 1076 to 1779 it also housed the Imperial Academy, Vietnam's first national university. Today it is a calm run of courtyards, old trees, trimmed lawns and red-and-tile roofs, which suits phone photography well. The grounds cover over 54,000 square metres, so there are plenty of different frames to try.

A good first photo is the three-arched entrance gate, Văn Miếu Môn, taken from outside, straight on along the central axis. Inside, the Khuê Văn pavilion (built in 1805, with a red upper storey and round windows) is the best-known building. Its reflection in the Thiên Quang well makes a lovely second shot. The other highlight is the row of stone doctoral stelae on turtle bases. Eighty-two survive, recording the names of 1,307 graduates from royal exams held between 1442 and 1779.

For your phone, keep the gate square-on and level, with the gridlines switched on. Inside, move slowly and look for lines: the stelae lead the eye towards the pavilion, and the courtyards give natural frames. Turn flash off in the worship halls. Wait for gaps between visitors, as the paths can fill up. The gate can be photographed from outside, but the pavilion, well and stelae are inside the compound, so check the official site before you go for current ticket and opening details.
text.geographic_location: The Temple of Literature is in central Hanoi, just south of the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long. It sits in its own walled grounds with the Văn lake and Giám park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long area and head south to the temple. Navigate to the main entrance gate, Văn Miếu Môn. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the gate straight on. If the full facade does not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Inside, the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) is good for details such as the stelae and turtle bases.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Văn Miếu Môn (in front of the main entrance gate, on the central axis). The three-arched entrance gate framed on its central axis, shot wide to include the gate's full facade. Outside the main entrance gate, on the central axis. This is the first photo stop. From the gate position the three-arched gate is framed centrally, and the temple grounds lie ahead to the north. Shoot wide enough to include the whole facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre yourself on the middle arch, keep the phone upright and level using the gridlines, and leave a little space above the roof. Once inside, if you have a ticket, try the Khuê Văn pavilion reflected in the Thiên Quang well, or the long line of stelae leading towards the central pavilion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the gate to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the facade does not wash out. Turn flash off inside the halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the sun lights the gate facade from the east.

text.access_note: The gate can be photographed from outside, but the temple compound is ticketed, so check the official site before you go for entry and opening details.

photo.artist: The original uploader was Chuoibk at English Wikipedia.

name: Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum
label: Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quảng trường Ba Đình' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quảng trường Ba Đình' (relation/21401560): middle (486 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37625751: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum' (61 m across).
notes: Marble memorial to Ho Chi Minh on Ba Đình Square.

text.description: The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum is a square building of grey granite with a sloping roof, standing in the middle of Ba Đình Square. It is about 21.6 metres high and 41.2 metres wide. Work began in 1973 and it was inaugurated in August 1975. The design drew on Lenin's Mausoleum in Moscow but adds a Vietnamese sloping roof. It photographs well because it is so simple: a calm, symmetrical front with the name carved above the portico, and wide lawns and a flagpole leading up to it. The lawn is laid out in green squares, which gives you tidy lines to work with. Two soldiers stand guard at the entrance, which adds a human figure to the frame. Photography is not allowed inside, so this is an outside-only spot. Keep the whole building in view, with the flagpole or lawn in front. Barriers and guards can close off parts of the square, so work with whatever view is open that day. A second option is the roadside along Đường Hùng Vương, where trees and the surrounding grounds frame the building.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Ba Đình Square in Hanoi. The Ho Chi Minh Museum and stilt house lie just to the west of the square, and Bắc Sơn Street runs away from the lawn towards the Martyrs' Memorial.
text.directions_text: From central Hanoi go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum on Ba Đình Square. Walk with the mausoleum straight ahead of you, to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want lawn and flagpole in the foreground, and keep the phone level so the sides of the building do not lean. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the inscription over the portico and the guards at the door.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Quảng trường Ba Đình (Open lawns on the front (north-facing) approach to the mausoleum). The full granite facade, with the lawns and flagpole in the foreground and the honor guard in the frame. The building is to the west, straight ahead of you. From here you can fit the full granite facade in the frame, with the lawns and flagpole in front and the honour guard at the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the building's base on the lower line. Place the flagpole or a path between the lawn squares so it leads the eye to the door. Keep the roof level and the building centred, because the design is symmetrical. For a different view, try the roadside on Đường Hùng Vương, where trees and the grounds frame the exterior.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the pale sky does not wash out the grey granite. Live Photos can catch the guard change, but be respectful and do not crowd the guards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the sun is low and the crowds are thinner. The flag-raising at the flagpole is at 6 a.m. in the hot season and 6:30 a.m. in the cold season. Late afternoon also gives softer light and fewer people. If you stay for the flag-lowering at 9 p.m., switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.

text.access_note: The square is an outdoor public space, but the mausoleum has set visiting times, closes each year for maintenance and has dress and behaviour rules inside, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hoàn Kiếm Lake
label: Hoàn Kiếm Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đinh Tiên Hoàng' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đinh Tiên Hoàng nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/198437: large area 'Hoàn Kiếm Lake' (680 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The heart of Hanoi, a lake ringed by walking paths.

text.description: Hoàn Kiếm Lake is a calm stretch of water of about 12 hectares in the historical centre of Hanoi, and it is one of the city's major scenic spots and a focal point of its public life. Its name means "Lake of the Returned Sword". The legend says Emperor Lê Lợi gave a magic sword back to a Golden Turtle God here after winning a war against Ming China. A small Turtle Tower on an islet near the middle of the lake is linked to that story. Near the northern shore, Jade Islet holds the Ngọc Sơn Temple, built in the 18th century. A wooden bridge painted vermilion red, the Huc Bridge (Thê Húc), joins the islet to the shore. Its name is poetically translated as "Perch of the Morning Sunlight". For a phone photo, the red bridge against the green water and the trees around the lake makes a simple, strong picture. Shoot from the street called Đinh Tiên Hoàng, facing the bridge, and let the bridge sit in the middle distance with the lake and trees around it. If you want a second picture, walk to Lê Thái Tổ for the Turtle Tower framed by shoreline trees. The statue of Emperor Lý Thái Tổ in Công viên Lý Thái Tổ also makes a quieter shot, with glimpses of the lake behind it. Expect crowds at sunrise and at weekends, so take a few frames and move on.
text.geographic_location: Hoàn Kiếm Lake lies in the historical centre of Hanoi and is one of the main focal points of the city's public life. Jade Islet and the Ngọc Sơn Temple sit near its northern shore.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are nearby, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the historical centre of Hanoi and ask for Hoàn Kiếm Lake. The lake itself lies to the west, about 2 minutes on foot from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the Huc Bridge sits small and clear in the middle distance. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more trees and sky around it. Use 2x or more to bring the bridge and Jade Islet closer without walking.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đinh Tiên Hoàng (lake's north/east shore, facing the Huc Bridge (sources disagree on which shore)). The vermilion Huc Bridge in the middle distance, leading to Ngoc Son Temple on Jade Island, with the lake and its trees around it. On the lake's eastern side, facing the Huc Bridge. Use the map to confirm the exact spot along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge on one of the lines so the water fills the foreground. Keep the horizon level. Wait for people to clear the pavement edge, or include a few for scale. For a different view, try Lê Thái Tổ for the Turtle Tower with the shoreline trees, or Công viên Lý Thái Tổ for the statue among the gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the red stays rich and the sky is not washed out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone still against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, or after dark when the bridge is lit. Both are popular, so expect crowds, especially at weekends.

text.access_note: The lake shore is an open public space and the temple ticket is not needed for the shore views; if you want to go onto Jade Islet or into Ngọc Sơn Temple, check the official site before you go.

name: Hỏa Lò Prison
label: Hỏa Lò Prison
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hai Bà Trưng' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Phố Hỏa Lò and Phố Hai Bà Trưng (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/340128580: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hoa Lo Prison' (129 m across).
notes: Former prison turned museum, nicknamed the 'Hanoi Hilton'.

text.description: Hỏa Lò Prison was built by the French between 1896 and 1901 and called Maison Centrale, or 'Central House'. It held Vietnamese political prisoners, and later, during the Vietnam War, American prisoners of war, who nicknamed it the 'Hanoi Hilton'. The name Hỏa Lò means 'stove', after the street where stove-sellers once traded. The prison was demolished in 1993-94, and only the gatehouse remains, as a museum. That makes the street frontage the part most visitors photograph. The old wall, the gate and the weathered brick give you a strong, plain subject, and the busy city around it adds a sense of scale and everyday life. The prison stood close to Hanoi's French Quarter, and from the street corner you see both that setting and the compound's edge. Take a few frames, some wide and some tighter on the gate. Stay on the pavement and keep an eye on the traffic while you line up the shot. Photography inside the museum is generally allowed in daytime, but flash and tripods are restricted and some areas are off-limits, so follow the staff's guidance.
text.geographic_location: In central Hanoi, on the edge of the French Quarter, at the corner where Hai Bà Trưng Street meets Hỏa Lò Street. The surviving gatehouse is on the street side of the old prison site.
text.directions_text: Head for the French Quarter in central Hanoi, then look for the corner of Hai Bà Trưng and Hỏa Lò streets. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Hỏa Lò Prison Museum (the gatehouse). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the wall, the gate and the street together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gate and sign without stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Phố Hỏa Lò and Phố Hai Bà Trưng (corner where Hai Bà Trưng meets Hỏa Lò, at the prison's gate side). The prison's street-facing wall and gate seen at an angle from the corner, with the surrounding street life of the French Quarter edge. The prison lies to the south-west of you. From here you see the street-facing wall and gate at an angle, with the street life of the French Quarter edge around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your phone's gridlines and place the wall along one line, so the gate sits off-centre and the street leads the eye towards it. Keep the verticals straight by holding the phone level. For a second view, walk along Hỏa Lò Street and shoot the brick entrance facade and gatehouse, with the Maison Centrale sign at the gate, framed from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. Live Photos can catch passing scooters, but wait for a gap in the traffic if you want a clean frame of the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is simplest for the street view, and earlier in the day is usually calmer. Check the museum's official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: The gatehouse is a museum, so entry may be ticketed and times may vary: check the official site before you go; the street corner itself is an ordinary public pavement.

name: Turtle Tower
label: Turtle Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đinh Tiên Hoàng' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Đinh Tiên Hoàng and Lê Thái Tổ (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Small moss-covered tower on an island in Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

text.description: Turtle Tower (Tháp Rùa) is a small, three-storey tower on an islet in the middle of Hoan Kiem Lake, right in the centre of Hanoi. It is one of the best-known sights of the city, and it photographs well because it stands alone on the water. You get a simple, calm picture: the grey tower, its reflection, the green lake around it and the roofs of the Old Quarter behind. The tower was built in 1886 in honour of Lê Lợi, the national hero linked to the lake's sword-and-turtle legend. In 1890 the French put a miniature Statue of Liberty on top, and it was taken down in 1945. The islet cannot be visited, so every shot is taken from the shore, and the tower looks small in a wide view. The ultra-wide lens will make it tiny, so use the telephoto lens and keep some lake in the foreground. Early or late in the day the reflection is usually calmer and the colours softer. Check the weekend walking-street schedule, as it can change how busy the shoreline is.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Hoan Kiem Lake in central Hanoi. Ngọc Sơn Temple and the red Thê Húc Bridge are also on the lake; confirm their exact position in a map app.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. The default lens (1x) works for a wider scene with more lake and rooftops. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the tower too small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Đinh Tiên Hoàng and Lê Thái Tổ (southern end of the lake, where the two streets meet). The tower on its islet across the water, with the lake in the foreground and the Old Quarter roofline behind it. The tower sits on its islet across the water to the south, with the lake in front and the Old Quarter roofline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on a third, leaving open water in front so the reflection shows. For a different view, walk to Cầu Thê Húc and put the red bridge in the foreground with the tower in the distance. Keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. At 3x or 5x, hold the phone with both hands and rest your elbows on something firm.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, for warm light on the tower and its reflection.

text.access_note: The tower is on an islet with no public access, so you photograph it from the lakeside; check the official site before you go if you want to visit anything on the lake itself.

name: Trấn Quốc Pagoda
label: Trấn Quốc Pagoda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đường Thanh Niên' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đường Thanh Niên nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/220302249: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tran Quoc Pagoda' (126 m across).
notes: Oldest pagoda in Hanoi, on an islet in West Lake.

text.description:
Trấn Quốc Pagoda is the oldest Buddhist temple in Hanoi. It sits on a small islet near the southeastern shore of West Lake, joined to the land by a short causeway. The red stupa, eleven tiers tall, rises above the trees, and the lake water around it gives you a calm, balanced picture.

The temple was first built in the sixth century, under Emperor Lý Nam Đế, and was moved to its present islet in 1615 when the Red River began to eat into its old site. The last major repairs were made in 1815. In the grounds there is also a Bodhi tree grown from a cutting of the tree at Bodh Gaya in India, given in 1959.

The classic photo is taken from the approach to the stone causeway on Đường Thanh Niên, looking towards the temple entrance and the stupa, with the lake filling the foreground. Late afternoon gives warm light on the red tower, but sunset is busy, so be ready to wait for a clear view. Early morning is quieter. The pagoda is an active place of worship, so keep your phone for the outside views, avoid flash, and do not photograph worshippers up close.
text.geographic_location: In Hanoi, on a small islet near the southeastern shore of West Lake (Hồ Tây), reached by a short causeway from Thanh Niên Road.
text.directions_text: There is no listed Underground or tram stop nearby, so use a map app to reach Thanh Niên Road (Đường Thanh Niên) on the southeastern shore of West Lake. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the stupa with lake water in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and sky, and keep the stupa away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the red tower alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đường Thanh Niên (stone causeway section looking toward the temple entrance and stupa). The red stupa framed by lake water in the foreground, the classic balanced composition from the approach to the islet. Look towards the temple entrance and the red stupa, with the lake in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the stupa on one of the vertical lines, with a strip of lake water along the bottom of the picture. Keep the tower upright by holding the phone level. For a different view, try the wide look across the lake from near Cầu Nhật Tân on the eastern bank, or the tower seen from below inside the grounds, framed by Bodhi branches or bonsai.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red stupa to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour at golden hour. Do not use flash. Take a few frames in a row, as people often walk across the causeway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon for golden-hour light, but expect crowds at sunset. Early morning is quieter and can bring mist over the lake.

text.access_note: The pagoda is an active place of worship, so cover your shoulders and knees and do not photograph inside the prayer halls or during ceremonies; access to the grounds at night may be restricted, so check opening hours locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep sky colour in late-afternoon light.
Cars, scooters or passers-by on the causeway may briefly spoil a frame, so taking several shots helps.

name: Hanoi Opera House
label: Hanoi Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quảng trường Cách mạng Tháng Tám' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quảng trường Cách Mạng Tháng Tám' (node/6611717983): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37933050: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Opera House' (98 m across).
notes: French colonial opera house in the Beaux-Arts style.

text.description:
The Hanoi Opera House is a grand theatre in the French colonial style, and it is one of the easiest buildings in the city to photograph. It was built between 1901 and 1911 and modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris, though smaller and with materials chosen to suit Hanoi's climate. The design is neoclassical with French Renaissance touches, so you get a row of columns, a decorated roofline and a balcony that sits in the middle of the frame. It seated 870 people. The balcony is also where Viet Minh leaders proclaimed independence in September 1945, and the square in front was the site of a huge rally in August of that year.

It photographs well because the square in front is open. You can step back far enough to fit the whole façade in one frame, with the columns and roofline clear of other buildings. After dark the façade is floodlit, which makes the evening one of the best times for pictures. Please note the Opera House has been closed for a two-year renovation since 31 January 2026. The outside and the square can still be photographed, but scaffolding or site fencing may affect your view, so confirm before going. If the square is too busy, you can also try the street corner on Lê Thánh Tông, next to the hotel, or the steps at Trang Tien Plaza across the street for a wide view.
text.geographic_location: In central Hanoi, at August Revolution Square, where Tràng Tiền street ends. The Hilton Hanoi Opera Hotel and the MGallery Hotel de l'Opera are its neighbours.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or train stops listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach August Revolution Square, at the head of Tràng Tiền street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building, and the default lens (1x) once you have backed away across the square. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the columns, balcony and roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Quảng trường Cách mạng Tháng Tám (open forecourt directly in front of the main façade). The full neoclassical façade, columns and roofline framed across the open square, especially lit up after dark. The open forecourt directly in front of the main façade. From here the full façade, columns and roofline fit across the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines, so the building doesn't lean. Keep the whole roofline in the frame and leave a little space of square in front. For a different angle, try the corner of Lê Thánh Tông next to the hotel, or the view from Trang Tien Plaza across the street, where steps and traffic add foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the floodlit stonework does not turn white. In the evening, hold your phone steady, or brace your arms against your body, and use night mode if your phone offers it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or sunset, when the façade is lit, or early morning if you want fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: The square in front is an open public space, but the Opera House itself is closed for renovation, so confirm the current status before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep vertical lines straight when photographing a tall building.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop bright floodlit surfaces from washing out.
Night mode needs a steady hand or bracing to avoid blur.
Ultra-wide lenses suit large buildings when you are standing close.

name: One Pillar Pagoda
label: One Pillar Pagoda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chùa Một Cột' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Chùa Một Cột' (way/697326496): middle (10 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Small 11th-century pagoda built on a single stone pillar.

text.description:
One Pillar Pagoda (Chùa Một Cột) is a small wooden shrine that sits on a single stone pillar rising from a lotus pond, shaped to look like a lotus blossom. The lotus is a Buddhist symbol of purity because it flowers in muddy water. Emperor Lý Thái Tông first built the pagoda in 1049, and it was perfected in 1105. It was destroyed in 1954 and rebuilt in 1955, so what you see is a careful restoration. The pillar is about 4 metres tall and 1.25 metres across, which makes the whole building look light and almost afloat.

It photographs well because the shape is so simple. One pillar, one curved roof and one pond give you a clean, balanced picture, and on a calm morning the pavilion sits above its own reflection. From the pond edge in front of the shrine you can centre the pillar and take the classic view. It is a small site, so you only need a few minutes for photos, but allow longer if the pond edge is busy. The edge is narrow and can be slippery after rain, so mind your footing while you line up the shot. If you want a quieter picture, the courtyard behind the pagoda gives a more distant view with trees around it.
text.geographic_location: One Pillar Pagoda is in Ba Đình district, in central Hanoi, near the Thăng Long Citadel. It lies in the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum area.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed nearby, so start from Ba Đình district, close to the Thăng Long Citadel and the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum area. Go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Chùa Một Cột (One Pillar Pagoda). The mausoleum area can have security restrictions, so be ready for your driver to drop you a short walk away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the pillar and roof sit naturally in the frame. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the pagoda near the centre so the edges do not stretch it. For the more distant courtyard view through the trees, try telephoto (2x or more) if your phone has it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (pond edge directly in front of the shrine, centred on the pillar). The wooden pavilion on its single stone pillar, centred above its reflection in the lotus pond. From here you see the wooden pavilion on its single stone pillar, centred above its reflection in the lotus pond. Step back along the edge a little so the whole pillar and roof fit in one frame. For a quieter, more distant view, try the courtyard behind the pagoda, with the pagoda framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the pillar on the central vertical line. Keep the phone level so the pillar stands straight. Leave space below for the reflection, and keep the pond edge out of the bottom corners. A second picture from the courtyard behind the pagoda gives a calmer, tree-framed version.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out the roof. Wait for ripples on the pond to settle before you take the shot. Do not use flash, because it is not allowed inside the shrine and does nothing for the pond view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, about 7–9 am, when the light is good and the pond is calmer. The pond edge gets crowded by mid-morning.

Thăng Long Water Puppet Theatre is on the lakeside street of Đinh Tiên Hoàng, and its red-and-gold front is the part worth photographing. After dark the building is lit, and it stands out well against the street behind it. That makes the evening the most rewarding time for a phone picture.

The classic view is from across the street, on the lake side, facing the facade. From there you can fit the whole lit front into one frame, with the street around it to give a sense of place. Keep your phone level and turn on the gridlines, so the building doesn't lean. Wait for a gap in the passers-by and take a few frames, because the pavement and road can be busy.

For a second picture, go up to the entrance. Costumed puppet characters are often on display there, with the decorated front behind them. They make a good close-up, and the best times to catch them are before and after a show. Please ask politely before photographing anyone beside the puppets.

Photo rules inside can vary. Check on the day whether a camera fee applies to ordinary photos or only to filming the show, so ask at the ticket desk before you shoot indoors. Flash is not allowed during performances, so switch it off. Fees and hours can change, so ask at the ticket desk before you go.
text.geographic_location: The theatre is on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, a lakeside street in Hanoi.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full lit front from across the street. If the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole building, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). For the puppet characters at the entrance, move close and use the default lens (1x) or a light zoom (2x).

Wait for a gap in the traffic and people before pressing the shutter. For a different picture, go to the entrance and take a close shot of the costumed puppet characters with the decorated front behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall. Tap the bright facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red and gold are not washed out. Keep flash off, as it is not allowed during performances.

name: Ngọc Sơn Temple
label: Ngọc Sơn Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đinh Tiên Hoàng' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đinh Tiên Hoàng nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/178995262: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ngoc Son Temple' (38 m across).
notes: Temple on an islet reached by the red Huc Bridge.

text.description:
Ngọc Sơn Temple sits on a small islet in Hoàn Kiếm Lake, right in central Hanoi. It was built in the early 19th century and was first dedicated to the "Three Sages"; the national hero Trần Hưng Đạo was later brought into the temple too. A red arched bridge, Thê Húc, leads out to the islet from the shore. The grounds also hold the Pen Tower (Tháp Bút), the ink-slab, the Đắc Nguyệt moon-viewing pavilion and the Trấn Ba pavilion, all of which carry symbolic meaning.

This spot photographs well because the scene is built in layers. From the lakeside path on Đinh Tiên Hoàng you can see the Thê Húc Bridge across the water, with the stone Pen Tower close by to use in the foreground. The still water and the bridge's red arch give you colour and a clear shape even on a hazy day. It is also a free place to stand, so you can take your time.

For a practical plan, take the main shot from the lake edge and then walk on to the bridge if you want to go in. Entering the temple grounds is ticketed, and photography is restricted inside the main hall and near the altar, so keep your phone away there. If you want a second angle, the south side of the lake gives the classic full view of the bridge leading to the temple island, with its reflection in the water.
text.geographic_location: In central Hanoi, on an islet in Hoàn Kiếm Lake.
text.directions_text: There are no stations listed close by, so head for Hoàn Kiếm Lake in central Hanoi and make your way to the northern shore on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, beside the Pen Tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the bridge, the water and the Pen Tower together. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge and temple roofs, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the Pen Tower to look tall and close.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đinh Tiên Hoàng (lakeside stretch near the Pen Tower (Tháp Bút), looking out toward the bridge). The Huc Bridge seen across the water from the lake edge, with the Pen Tower stone pillar as a foreground element. From here the temple island and the Thê Húc Bridge are to the south across the water, with the Pen Tower stone pillar close by as a foreground element.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Pen Tower on one side of the frame, with the red bridge leading across the water on the other. Keep the horizon level so the lake edge doesn't slope. If you want a different view, the south shore of the lake gives a classic full shot of the bridge and temple island with the reflection, and the bridge itself puts the red arch in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body for a couple of seconds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 6 PM is suggested for golden-hour light, and early morning also works for the bridge at sunrise. Check the actual light on the day, as these times come from visitor tips.

text.access_note: The lakeside path is an open public street, but entering the temple grounds is ticketed and photography is restricted inside the main hall, so check the official site before you go.

name: Đồng Xuân Market
label: Đồng Xuân Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chợ Đồng Xuân' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1212230635: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dong Xuan Market' (230 m across).
notes: Largest covered market, at the north end of the Old Quarter.

text.description:
Đồng Xuân is the largest covered market in Hanoi, and its front is one of the most photographed spots in the area. The French administration built the first market here in 1889, and its best-known feature is the five-arch entrance, corresponding to the market's five domes. A fire in 1994 nearly destroyed the market, and it was partly rebuilt in its original form. What you see today is a mix of old design and busy modern wholesale trade.

The front photographs well because it has a clear, symmetrical shape with real street life in front of it: motorbikes, vendors and shoppers. That gives you the classic full-facade shot with plenty going on at street level. Standing outside is also easier than shooting inside. The interior is crowded, and vendors may not want to be photographed, so ask before pointing your phone at a stall.

Keep the five arches centred and keep your phone upright so the vertical lines stay straight. Traffic is constant, so be patient and take several frames, and watch for passing motorbikes as you step back. If you want a different view, the elevated walkway known in the Vietnamese press as the glass bridge (cầu kính) looks down over the market front and the street. Check its exact name on the map before heading there.
text.geographic_location: Đồng Xuân Market is in the Old Quarter of Hanoi, in Hoàn Kiếm district, roughly 600 m north of Hoàn Kiếm Lake. It sits in the Đồng Xuân ward, one of the busiest trading areas in the city.
text.directions_text: There is no station listed close to the market, so start from Hoàn Kiếm Lake and head north through the Old Quarter. The market is roughly 600 m north of the lake, though the walking route through the Old Quarter will be a little longer than that. As a rough guess, allow somewhere around 10 to 15 minutes on foot. You can also go by taxi or hired scooter and ask to be dropped at Chợ Đồng Xuân. Đồng Xuân Market is the subject, and its middle is inside the building, so for the full-facade shot walk to the street outside the main entrance and face the facade. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full five-arch front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or crowds stop you stepping back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the arches, signs or vendors with their goods.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Chợ Đồng Xuân is the subject, and its middle is inside the building. For the full-facade shot, step out to the street in front of the entrance and face the five arches. From there you get the market's five-arch front with street traffic and vendors in the foreground, the classic full-facade shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre arch up with the middle of the frame. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. Leave some street in the bottom of the picture for the motorbikes and vendors. For a higher, downward view of the market front and the crowds below, try the glass bridge (cầu kính chợ Đồng Xuân) as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the building does not look washed out. Take a few quick shots or a Live Photo so you can pick the frame with the best gap in the traffic. Ask before photographing people or stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the facade, and early in the day may be calmer on the street. On Friday to Sunday evenings the street in front has been closed to traffic for the night market, so it can be easier to frame and well lit. Check locally that this still applies. After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady.

text.access_note: The front of the market is on a public street and open to view, but opening times for the market and the night market can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long
label: Imperial Citadel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đoan Môn' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Đoan Môn' (way/696389268): middle (82 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.

text.description:
The Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long is the old royal enclosure of Hanoi, set in the middle of the city in Ba Đình District. Building began in 1010 under Emperor Lý Thái Tổ and finished in early 1011, and it stayed the seat of the Vietnamese court until 1789. Much of it was later pulled down under the French, so what you see today is a mix of surviving gates, restored buildings and open archaeological ground. The central sector became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.

For photos, start at Đoan Môn, the main gate. Its full front facade sits against open sky, with the citadel grounds stretching out behind it, so it makes a clean, strong picture even with a phone. Stand on the south side, facing the entrance, and give yourself room to step back. Inside, the stone dragon balustrades on the steps of Điện Kính Thiên reward a closer look, and the pavilion Hậu Lâu gives a quieter view of the citadel walls when the steps are busy.

The site is large and open, so you can move around to avoid other visitors. Some areas may be closed for archaeological work or event set-ups, which can block views, so be ready to adjust your angle on the day.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Hanoi, in Ba Đình District.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop for this spot. From the centre of Hanoi, go by taxi or hired scooter to the citadel in Ba Đình District and head for the main gate, Đoan Môn, on the south side. The rest of the citadel grounds lie behind it to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole gate when you are close, and the default lens (1x) from further back for a more natural look. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x) for the carved dragons at Điện Kính Thiên.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main gate, south side facing the entrance). The gate's full front facade framed against the sky, with the citadel's grounds stretching behind it. From here the gate's full front facade is framed against the sky, with the citadel grounds stretching away behind it to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the gate up square so the roofline stays level. Keep a band of sky above it and let the grounds show behind. If the steps at Điện Kính Thiên are crowded, try Hậu Lâu for a quieter view of the citadel walls. For the dragon balustrades, use the telephoto and fill the frame with the carving.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the grounds are quiet and the light falls on the gate from the east. Sunrise or sunset can also give strong shadows.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed heritage site with its own opening days, and some areas may be closed for archaeological work or events, so check the official site before you go.

name: St. Joseph's Cathedral, Hanoi
label: St. Joseph's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Phố Nhà Thờ' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Phố Nhà Thờ nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28912942: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Joseph Cathedral' (78 m across).

text.description: St. Joseph's Cathedral is a grey Gothic Revival church in the Old Quarter, and this view shows it as part of the street rather than as a monument on its own. The two square towers rise above the cafés and shopfronts, so the church sits in the middle of everyday Hanoi life. The towers are about 31 m high, and each holds five bells. They are often compared with the towers of Notre Dame in Paris, which the architects were trying to echo. Building began in 1884 and the cathedral was consecrated in December 1886, which makes it the oldest church in Hanoi. It stands on the site of the old Báo Thiên Pagoda. Its exterior was restored in a major renovation between July 2020 and May 2022. For a phone photo, the street gives you natural framing: shopfronts and signs on both sides lead the eye to the towers. Expect people and scooters to pass through the foreground, so take a few frames and pick the one with the best gaps. The front square can be busy on Sunday evenings, when large crowds gather for the 6:00 PM Mass. It is sometimes used for events with a stage, which can block the view.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Quarter of Hoàn Kiếm District, Hanoi, in a small square just west of Hoàn Kiếm Lake.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from Hoàn Kiếm Lake and walk west into the Old Quarter towards the cathedral area. Find Phố Nhà Thờ, the street that ends at the cathedral square, and walk to the far end from the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the towers and the street both fit in the frame. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer and make them look larger above the shopfronts. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move into the square and want the whole façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Phố Nhà Thờ (far end of the street, looking back toward the cathedral). The towers rising above the cafés and shopfronts of the street, so the church sits inside everyday Old Quarter life. At the far end of the street, and look back toward the cathedral. The towers should rise above the cafés and shopfronts, with the cathedral to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the towers near the centre, with the street's edges leading toward them. Hold the phone level so the towers don't lean. Leave some shopfronts and signs in the frame, because they make this view different from the straight-on photo. For that straight-on view, with the full façade, both towers and the rose window, go into the cathedral square. Phố Nhà Chung is another good street for the towers with passers-by and scooters in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a short burst or a few frames while people and scooters pass, then choose the cleanest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day, as the direction the façade faces affects when it is best lit. Avoid Sunday evening around the 6:00 PM Mass if you want a clear view, as crowds gather in the square and the street.

text.access_note: Photographing the outside from the street and square is free and open to everyone, but the interior is limited by Mass times and the main gates are generally opened only during Mass, so check the official site before you go.

name: Long Biên Bridge
label: Long Biên Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đường Trần Nhật Duật' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đường Trần Nhật Duật nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/874082896: large area 'Long Biên Bridge' (1737 m across): the middle of the area.
notes: Historic steel cantilever bridge over the Red River.

text.description:
Long Biên Bridge is a long steel cantilever bridge across the Red River, linking Hanoi's Hoàn Kiếm and Long Biên districts. It was built between 1899 and 1902 and opened in 1903, when it was called Paul Doumer Bridge. At about 2.4 km, it was then one of the longest bridges in Asia. It was bombed heavily during the Vietnam War, and only about half of it keeps its original shape. Repairs show in the mix of old and newer girders.

That patched-up look is what makes it photograph well. The steel framework is dramatic on its own, and it gets better when a train crosses, because trains, mopeds, bicycles and pedestrians all still use it. For the classic picture, stand on Đường Trần Nhật Duật, on the stretch facing the bridge's Hanoi-side approach. Guides rate it highly for getting the girders and a moving train into one frame, and it works best around sunrise or sunset, when low golden light throws strong shadows.

Trains cross several times a day and the girders shake as they pass. Keep to the pedestrian lanes and never stand on the rails. For a different view, walk onto the bridge itself to look along the receding lattice with the river below. The mid-river sandbar, Bãi Giữa, gives a view of the whole bridge reflected in the water, but only go in the dry season, never after heavy rain, and not alone after dark.
text.geographic_location: Long Biên Bridge crosses the Red River on the north-east side of central Hanoi, linking Hoàn Kiếm district on the city side with Long Biên district on the far bank.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed nearby, so start from central Hoàn Kiếm and go by taxi or hired scooter to Đường Trần Nhật Duật, on the stretch facing the bridge's Hanoi-side approach. Ask your driver to drop you at the street rather than on the bridge itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the girders and the train into one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull a passing train closer to the steelwork. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you walk onto the bridge to stretch the lattice into the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đường Trần Nhật Duật (stretch facing the bridge's Hanoi-side approach). The bridge from the street with a passing train, with the steel structure and the train in one frame. On the stretch facing the bridge's Hanoi-side approach. The photo shows the bridge from the street with a passing train, the steel structure and the train in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge's steel structure along one third of the frame, leaving room for the train to cross. Take a few shots as the train approaches rather than waiting for one perfect moment. For an alternative, the view along the bridge itself shows the steel lattice receding above the river, and the sandbar Bãi Giữa gives a reflected view of the whole bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the train to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the steel stays dark and the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo as the train passes, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when golden light casts strong shadows across the steelwork.

text.access_note: The street is an open public place, and the bridge is shared with trains, so keep to the pedestrian lanes and check the official site before you go for any restoration work or restrictions.

name: Ba Đình Square
label: Ba Đình Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quảng trường Ba Đình' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quảng trường Ba Đình' (relation/21401560): middle (486 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21401560: 'Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum', the best-known feature inside 'Ba Dinh Square' (488 m across).
notes: Large square where Ho Chi Minh read the 1945 independence declaration.

text.description:
Ba Đình Square is the broad ceremonial heart of Hanoi. It is where Ho Chi Minh read the Proclamation of Independence on 2 September 1945, and it takes its name from the Ba Đình Uprising against the French in 1886-1887. After his death the granite Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum was built on the square, and it is still a major place of tourism and pilgrimage. The square is about 488 m across, with the President's Palace, the National Assembly Building and several ministries around it.

It photographs well because of its scale and order. Wide lawns, a tall flagpole and the pale, strongly shaped granite facade make a clean, simple picture with plenty of sky. The classic frame is from the southern end of the square, looking north, with the flagpole in the foreground and the mausoleum rising over the lawns beyond. Early in the day the facade is lit from the front rather than backlit, and some guides say the square is less crowded before about 9 a.m.

If you can, also catch the morning flag-raising, when guards in white uniforms stand out against the open space. For a view across the whole square, especially when an event fills it, the guides suggest Phố Hùng Vương, though that view depends on a café or hotel. Keep your phone away from the mausoleum interior, as photography is not allowed inside.
text.geographic_location: Ba Đình Square is in the centre of Ba Đình District in Hanoi, with the President's Palace, the National Assembly Building and several government ministries around it. The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum stands on the square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so get to the centre of Ba Đình District and walk to the square, looking for Ba Đình Square (Quảng trường Ba Đình). From there the mausoleum is about 117 m to the west, roughly 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the flagpole and the mausoleum facade together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full spread of the lawns, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the guards or flag-raising.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Quảng trường Ba Đình (southern end, by the flagpole, facing north toward the mausoleum). The mausoleum's granite facade rising over the lawns, with the tall flagpole in the foreground. The classic frame with the tall flagpole in the foreground and the mausoleum rising over the lawns comes from the southern end of the square, looking north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the flagpole on one vertical line, with the facade filling the middle band and the lawns below. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. For an alternative, try Phố Hùng Vương for a wide panorama of the whole square; this view depends on a café or hotel.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the pale granite keeps its detail and the sky stays blue. Try a Live Photo during the flag-raising to catch the movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 9 a.m., when the mausoleum is lit from the front rather than backlit and the square is said to be less crowded.

text.access_note: The square and gardens are generally open for photographs, but the mausoleum has security screening, a dress code and bag restrictions, bans photography inside, and has closing days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Quán Thánh Temple
label: Quán Thánh Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Thanh Niên' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Thanh Niên nearest the subject (our map tiles).

notes: Ancient Taoist temple near West Lake.

text.description: Quán Thánh Temple is a Taoist temple beside West Lake, dedicated to Trấn Vũ, a guardian deity of the north. Tradition dates it to the 11th century, and it is one of the Four Sacred Temples said to protect the old capital. It photographs well because several simple pictures sit close together: the main gate and roofline, the lake behind the entrance, and a shaded courtyard under a giant banyan tree. Inside the shrine is a large black bronze statue of Trấn Vũ, cast in 1677. It stands almost four metres tall and shows the deity with a serpent and a turtle. The gate and shrine were last rebuilt in 1893, so the buildings mix several imperial-era styles. That mix gives you plenty of roof ridges and carved detail to frame. For the classic view, stand on the lakeside road and shoot towards the entrance, so the gate and roof fill the foreground and the water sits behind them. The temple is still used for worship, and local people come in numbers around Tết and on the first and fifteenth of each lunar month. Keep out of worshippers' way, and don't photograph people while they pray. Turn off the flash near altars. Take your time in the courtyard, where the banyan's shade makes for softer, easier pictures than the open road.
text.geographic_location: In Quán Thánh Ward in Hanoi, on the corner of Quán Thánh Street and Thanh Niên Street, facing West Lake. It is a short walk from Trúc Bạch Lake.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is to come from central Hanoi by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Quán Thánh Temple on Thanh Niên Street, beside West Lake. If you are already by Trúc Bạch Lake, it is a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and roofline with the lake behind. If you need to fit the whole gate in from the roadside, try the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ridges and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Thanh Niên (slightly south of the temple, on the lakeside road, facing the entrance). The main gate and roofline in front, with West Lake water behind the entrance. The temple lies just to the east. From here you see the main gate and roofline in front, with West Lake water behind the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the gate and roof on the lower third, so the lake and sky add depth behind. Keep the phone level so the roof lines stay straight. For variety, try the three-door stone gate with its bell tower against the trees, or go into the courtyard for the banyan tree, roof ridges and sanctuary behind. Stay clear of worshippers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus. If the lake makes the sky bright and the temple dark, slide the exposure slider down a little. No flash near altars.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when light falls from the east at this angle.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship: remove your shoes before the raised prayer areas, keep clear of worshippers, and check the official site before you go for any photo rules or fees inside the main shrine.

name: Presidential Palace, Hanoi
label: Presidential Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hùng Vương' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Hùng Vương nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37629570: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Presidential Palace' (63 m across).
notes: Yellow French colonial palace seen from outside the gates.

text.description:
The Presidential Palace is a bright yellow, French colonial building that looks far more European than Vietnamese. It was built between 1900 and 1906 as the home of the French governor-general of Indochina. Its Italian Renaissance details include classical columns, broken pediments and a grand staircase up to the main floor. It stands behind wrought-iron gates with sentry boxes on either side, and the only obvious local touch is the mango trees in the grounds. After 1954 Ho Chi Minh is said to have chosen not to live in it. He built a traditional Vietnamese stilt house and a carp pond in the gardens instead. Today the palace is used for state occasions, and the building itself is closed to visitors.

It photographs well because the strong yellow wall, the black ironwork and the green trees make a clean, colourful composition. From the street you can take in the whole facade at once. Photographing the front from outside the gates may be restricted, and most views are taken from the side, though guides recommend the facade from outside, so check on the day. Photography near security posts is not allowed, so do not point your phone at security posts or restricted areas. Signs on the day decide, and take priority over anything written here. The garden paths, Mango Alley and the fish pond make lovely pictures if the grounds are open, but the grounds may need a ticket and are not open every day, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In central Hanoi, on the street frontage at 2 Hùng Vương. It is close to the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum area, which is near the palace, or from central Hanoi by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped at 2 Hùng Vương. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the gates and want the whole facade and the ironwork in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the columns and pediments without stepping closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hùng Vương (outside the palace gates, on the street frontage of the palace at 2 Hùng Vương). The bright yellow front facade of the palace with its wrought-iron gates, taken from the street outside the grounds. From the street frontage you see the bright yellow front of the palace behind its wrought-iron gates, with the building to the west. Check any signs first, and check on the day whether photographing the front is allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the gates up with the bottom third of the frame, so the yellow facade fills the middle. Keep the building straight by holding the phone level, not tilted up. If the grounds are open, Mango Alley is a good second picture: the yellow walls under a canopy of mango trees, with patches of light and shade on the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the yellow wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the yellow stays rich and does not wash out. Hold the phone steady and keep security posts out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light falls well on the facade.

text.access_note: The palace building is closed to visitors, photographing the front from outside may be restricted, photography is not allowed near security posts, and the grounds may be ticketed and open only on certain days, so check the official site and any signs on the day before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep strong yellow walls from looking washed out in bright light.
The 0.5x ultra-wide lens is useful for fitting the whole facade and gates into the frame when standing close to the street frontage.
Mango Alley and the fish pond are inside the palace grounds, so they can only be photographed when the grounds are open.

name: Vietnam National Museum of History
label: National History Museu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bảo tàng Lịch sử Quốc gia' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bảo tàng Lịch sử Quốc gia Việt Nam' (way/37933256): middle (201 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37933256: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum of Vietnamese History' (201 m across).
notes: French-Indochinese style building with Vietnamese history exhibits.

text.description:
The Vietnam National Museum of History is a pale yellow building whose tiered red roof and cupola give it the outline of a pagoda. It was built as the Musée Louis-Finot, a branch of the French School of the Far East, which opened in 1910 and was redesigned between 1925 and 1932 by the architects Ernest Hébrard and Charles Batteur. The result blends French colonial and traditional Vietnamese design, a mix known as "style Indochinois". It became a public museum in 1958 and now holds around 200,000 items, from the Stone Age to the 1945 revolution.

For photographs, the best view is at the front of the main entrance at 1 Tràng Tiền. Two golden dragon heads stand there, and they make a strong foreground against the yellow walls and the red roof behind. The double walls and balconies, which were designed to keep the building cool, add layers of shadow to the facade in daylight. Rooftop and balcony details are also worth a closer shot.

The museum sits just behind the Hanoi Opera House, so you can combine the two in one short walk. You can take the exterior shots from the front without going inside. Entry to the galleries is ticketed, and photography rules inside may differ from outside, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Hoan Kiem district, central Hanoi, at 1 Tràng Tiền Street, just behind the Hanoi Opera House.
text.directions_text: Head for the Hanoi Opera House in Hoan Kiem district and walk round to the back, where the museum's yellow facade fronts Tràng Tiền Street. The address is 1 Tràng Tiền Street, behind the Hanoi Opera House. Walk to the front of the main entrance, where the two golden dragon heads stand. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade, the roof and both dragon heads in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for roof tiles and balcony details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the main entrance at 1 Tràng Tiền, with the two golden dragon head sculptures). The yellow Indochinese main facade with its tiered red roof, framed by the two golden dragon heads in front of the entrance. Move to the front of the main entrance, between the two golden dragon heads, for the framed view. From here the photo shows the yellow Indochinese facade with its tiered red roof, framed by the two golden dragon heads in front of the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put one dragon head in the lower corner of the frame and let the facade and red roof rise behind it, or centre the entrance between the two dragons for a symmetrical shot. Turn on gridlines and keep the phone upright and level so the walls don't lean inwards. If the entrance is busy, wait a moment for a gap or take a tighter telephoto shot of the roof instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and the golden dragons keep their detail and the colours stay rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight hours, when the exterior is well lit. Sunlight and shadows on the facade add depth.

text.access_note: The museum is a ticketed site with its own photography rules inside, so check the official site for opening days, tickets and photo rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps stop the walls leaning inwards in a wide shot.
The entrance area can be busy with visitors at times.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep detail in bright sky and gilded sculptures.
The exterior can be photographed from the front without entering the galleries.

name: Flag Tower of Hanoi
label: Flag Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Điện Biên Phủ' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Điện Biên Phủ nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/184959290: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Flag Tower of Hanoi' (64 m across).
notes: 33 m tower from 1812, a surviving part of the old citadel.

text.description: The Flag Tower of Hanoi (Cột cờ Hà Nội) is one of the city's best-known symbols. It stands on Điện Biên Phủ street in Ba Đình District, and it once belonged to the Hanoi Citadel. It is a good subject for a phone because the shape is so clear. Three square brick tiers step upwards, a pyramid-shaped tower sits on top, and the red national flag flies above that. The tower is 33.4 m high, or 41 m including the flag. It is thought to date from 1805 or 1812, when it served as an observation post for the citadel, and it came through the French attack of 1896-1897 without being destroyed. Step back from the tower so the whole silhouette fits against the sky, with the flag at the top. The tower lies to the north-east of that spot. If you want a closer look, the thick brick walls and arched gateways of the lower terraces make good detail shots. The tower is in the old Vietnam Military History Museum grounds, and access to the inside and the upper levels can change, so plan on photographing the outside.
text.geographic_location: In Ba Đình District, central Hanoi, on Điện Biên Phủ street. The tower stands within the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long area.
text.directions_text: Head to Điện Biên Phủ street in Ba Đình District and ask for Cột cờ Hà Nội. From there the tower is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the street so the whole tower and the flag fit in. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand closer, or in Lenin Park, to include the tiered base. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the flag against the sky or for the brick terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Điện Biên Phủ (step back from the tower toward the street). The tower's silhouette against the sky, with the red national flag at the top. The tower is to the north-east of you. From here the photo shows the tower's silhouette against the sky, with the red national flag at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and hold the phone upright, keeping the tower straight and centred, with sky above the flag. Keep the phone level, because tilting it back will make the tower lean. For an alternative, try Lenin Park for a wide view of the whole tower framed by trees. For detail, try a close-up of the stacked terraces and arched gateways.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the flag stays red. Try Live Photos if the flag is moving in the wind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is the most pleasant time, with soft light on the brick. Late afternoon is also a good choice.

text.access_note: The tower stands in the former Vietnam Military History Museum grounds and may be ticketed or closed to visitors, with the interior and upper levels possibly shut, so check the official site before you go; the outside can generally be photographed.

name: Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi
label: Metropole Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ngô Quyền' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ngô Quyền nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7553773: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic colonial luxury hotel from 1901.

text.description:
The Sofitel Legend Metropole is a white colonial hotel on Ngô Quyền Street. It opened in August 1901 as the Grand Métropole Hôtel and was then the largest and most modern hotel in French Indochina. It is one of the most prominent surviving examples of French colonial architecture in Indochina. That is why it makes such a tidy phone photo: the pale front, the green shutters and the white portico with the hotel's name make a strong, symmetrical picture that is easy to read on a small screen.

The hotel has plenty of stories attached. Somerset Maugham stayed in 1923, Charlie Chaplin and Paulette Goddard honeymooned here in 1936, and Graham Greene stayed in 1951. Today's hotel was rebuilt and reopened in 1992. A newer Opera Wing was added later, and it faces the Hanoi Opera House across the junction on Lý Thái Tổ Street.

For the classic shot, stay on the public pavement and take in the whole façade. The courtyard, pool and interior are for guests, so please do not go into the grounds for pictures. If you have time, walk round to Lý Thái Tổ for a second frame that puts the newer wing beside the Opera House. Pavements can be busy with cars, scooters and people, so look around before you step back for a wider shot.
text.geographic_location: In central Hanoi, on Ngô Quyền Street, close to the Hanoi Opera House. The hotel's newer wing fronts Lý Thái Tổ Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Ngô Quyền Street using your phone's map. Once you are on the street, the hotel is the big white colonial building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow, because it will fit the whole front and portico into the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, with less stretching at the edges. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the engraved name and the green shutters.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ngô Quyền (in front of the main entrance and white portico of the Heritage Wing). The 1901 white colonial façade with green shutters and the portico, with the hotel's name on it, filling the frame. Shift a step or two until the façade sits well in your frame in front of the portico of the Heritage Wing. Stay on the public street and do not enter the hotel grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and, if the portico is visible from where you stand, line it up with the centre line so the façade looks straight. Keep your phone level to avoid leaning walls, and include a little pavement at the bottom for scale. For a second view, walk to Lý Thái Tổ for the newer Opera Wing set against the Hanoi Opera House.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the white does not turn grey or burn out. Switch off the flash, and use night mode in the evening, holding the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: As a general suggestion, soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to a white façade than midday sun. Check the light and how busy it is when you arrive.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed from the public street; the courtyard, pool and interior are for hotel guests only, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.
